name: FDI Screening Regulation
impact_assessment: none (2017 proposal was not accompanied by an impact assessment)
evidence_rating: moderate: Commission evaluation, ECA audit and OECD review on process; two independent quasi-experimental studies on investment flows (working papers) that point to some chilling effect of screening
summary: The FDI Screening Regulation set no measurable targets beyond a review. By 2024, 24 of 27 countries screened foreign investments and handled over 3,000 cases, blocking about 1% of those formally screened; the Commission's 2024 evaluation says the system protects security without deterring investment, while EU auditors found 'blind spots'. Independent studies suggest screening reduces foreign takeovers in newly screened sectors by roughly 12-16%, so the claim of no chilling effect is contested; a revised Regulation was adopted in 2026.

indicators.indicator: Commission report on the application of the Regulation within three years of entry into force (no quantified indicators; LFS specific objectives 'not applicable')
indicators.evidence: Delivered: evaluation SWD(2024) 23 (Jan 2024) plus five annual reports (latest COM(2025) 632). Led to a revised Regulation agreed Dec 2025 and adopted in 2026, replacing 2019/452.

indicators.objective: Identify and address FDI risks to security or public order affecting several Member States
indicators.indicator: Coverage of national screening mechanisms; cases handled through cooperation mechanism
indicators.evidence: Measured as activity: 24 of 27 Member States had screening laws by end-2024 (ECA counted six without in 2023). In 2024, 477 notifications from 21 Member States; Commission closed 92% in Phase 1 and issued opinions in under 2%. National authorities handled 3,136 cases; of formally screened cases 86% cleared unconditionally, 9% conditioned, ~1% blocked. ECA judged the framework only 'partially effective' with 'blind spots'.

indicators.objective: Maintain an open investment environment (no chilling of FDI)
indicators.evidence: Mixed. The Commission's 2024 evaluation states the Regulation 'has not had chilling effects' on FDI inflows (not backed by a causal test). Independent staggered DiD evidence finds national screening cuts cross-border M&A in newly screened sectors by about 12-16% (Eichenauer & Wang 2024), and EU countries adopting screening in line with the EU framework saw larger declines in M&A (Mau 2023). EU FDI inflows fell 23% in 2023 and 8.4% in 2024, driven by many factors.

indicators.objective: Administrative burden reasonable for authorities and investors
indicators.evidence: Evaluation found burden 'reasonable' based on stakeholder views; ECA found many low-risk or ineligible notifications overburden the mechanism. Not quantified.

literature.citation: European Commission (2024), Evaluation of Regulation (EU) 2019/452 establishing a framework for the screening of foreign direct investments into the Union (executive summary SWD(2024) 24), SWD(2024) 23
literature.title: Evaluation of Regulation (EU) 2019/452 establishing a framework for the screening of foreign direct investments into the Union (executive summary SWD(2024) 24)
literature.method: review (OECD study, ECA report, stakeholder consultation)
literature.headline: Positive impact on protecting security and public order; 'has not had chilling effects on the flow of FDI into the EU'; burden reasonable; blind spots from Member States without screening, intra-EU structured investments outside scope, short timelines and divergent national rules
literature.summary_plain: The Commission concluded that the screening framework helps protect security without deterring investment, but has gaps because some countries do not screen and national rules differ.
literature.quality: self-evaluation; no causal test of chilling effect

literature.citation: European Commission (2025), Fifth Annual Report on the screening of foreign direct investments into the Union, COM(2025) 632
literature.title: Fifth Annual Report on the screening of foreign direct investments into the Union
literature.headline: 2024: 477 notifications from 21 Member States (488 in 2023); 92% closed in Phase 1; Commission opinions in <2% of cases; 3,136 national cases (1,808 in 2023); 86% of screened cases cleared unconditionally, 9% with conditions, ~1% blocked; 24 Member States with screening legislation; EU FDI inflows down 8.4% in 2024
literature.summary_plain: In 2024 EU countries handled over 3,000 screening cases and blocked about 1% of those formally screened; the Commission cleared 92% of cross-border notifications within 15 days.

literature.citation: European Court of Auditors (2023), Screening foreign direct investments in the EU: First steps taken, but significant limitations remain in addressing security and public-order risks effectively, Special Report 27/2023
literature.title: Screening foreign direct investments in the EU: First steps taken, but significant limitations remain in addressing security and public-order risks effectively
literature.method: audit (sample of notified cases, all Commission opinions 2020-2022)
literature.headline: Commission took appropriate steps, but 'significant limitations' reduce effectiveness: six Member States lacked screening, divergent scope create 'multiple blind spots'; cooperation mechanism only 'partially effective'; high volume of low-risk cases overburdens it
literature.summary_plain: The EU's auditors found the framework a useful first step but riddled with blind spots because several countries did not screen investments at all.

literature.citation: OECD (2022), Framework for Screening Foreign Direct Investment into the EU: Assessing effectiveness and efficiency, OECD Publishing (study for the European Commission)
literature.title: Framework for Screening Foreign Direct Investment into the EU: Assessing effectiveness and efficiency
literature.venue: OECD Publishing (study for the European Commission)
literature.method: desk research and interviews with authorities
literature.headline: Positive overall assessment but 12 issues diminish effectiveness or efficiency, first among them Member States without any screening mechanism; reforms suggested for each
literature.summary_plain: An OECD review for the Commission judged the system broadly positive but listed 12 weaknesses, starting with countries that had no screening at all.
literature.quality: process evaluation; co-financed by the EU

literature.citation: Eichenauer & Wang (2024), Mild Deglobalization: Foreign Investment Screening and Cross-Border Investment, Kiel Working Paper 2265
literature.title: Mild Deglobalization: Foreign Investment Screening and Cross-Border Investment
literature.method: causal: staggered triple-difference (deal-level cross-border M&A, OECD and EU countries, 2007-2022)
literature.headline: Introducing screening reduces the number of M&A in a newly screened sector by 11.7-16.0%; driven by minority acquisitions and by deals involving foreign governments/SOEs or US investors; no reduction for intra-EU/EFTA deals
literature.summary_plain: The first cross-country study finds that when a sector becomes subject to investment screening, foreign takeovers in it fall by roughly 12-16%.
literature.quality: measures national screening, not the EU Regulation alone

literature.citation: Mau (2023), Screening or deterring investments into the European Union?, Maastricht University SBE blog (summary of working paper Mau 2023)
literature.title: Screening or deterring investments into the European Union?
literature.venue: Maastricht University SBE blog (summary of working paper Mau 2023)
literature.method: regression analysis of M&A by non-EU buyers in EU countries adopting screening mechanisms
literature.headline: EU countries adopting a screening mechanism in line with the EU framework saw significantly larger decreases in overall M&A activity; cannot confirm the effect is driven by Chinese or state-controlled investors
literature.summary_plain: An early study finds that EU countries which introduced screening under the EU framework saw bigger drops in foreign takeovers, and not only from China.
literature.quality: early results; full paper not reviewed

literature.authors: Eichenauer, V. Z.; Köppl, S.; Köppl-Turyna, M.
literature.title: Investment screening and venture capital
literature.venue: EcoAustria Research Paper No. 30 (also Kiel Working Paper 2282 / CESifo WP 11538)
literature.method: panel regressions on cross-border VC deals (Preqin) linked to country-sector screening coverage (PRISM data extended by Eichenauer & Wang), Europe 2007-2022
literature.outcomes: number, size and structure of cross-border venture capital deals
literature.headline: Despite very few deals actually being blocked, the spread of investment screening is associated with a significant decline in cross-border VC deals in Europe, strongest for financial investors, late-stage rounds and non-OECD investors.
literature.summary_plain: When European countries started checking foreign investments for security risks, fewer foreign venture capital investors put money into European start-ups, even though almost no deals were actually stopped.
literature.quality: Panel design exploiting staggered national screening reforms; measures national regimes around the EU framework rather than Regulation 2019/452 alone; exact effect sizes not in abstract
literature.citation: Eichenauer, V. Z.; Köppl, S.; Köppl-Turyna, M. (2024), Investment screening and venture capital, EcoAustria Research Paper No. 30 (also Kiel Working Paper 2282 / CESifo WP 11538)

literature.authors: Kaya, O.; Mostowfi, M.; Sugandhita, S.
literature.title: Foreign investment screening and cross-border M&A in sensitive sectors: Evidence from Germany
literature.method: difference-in-differences on firm-level M&A data (newly regulated vs other sectors), Germany 2016-2024
literature.outcomes: likelihood and type of foreign acquisitions of German firms by investor origin
literature.headline: Germany's 2020 screening reform significantly raised the likelihood that German firms in newly regulated sectors were acquired by investors from other EU countries, driven by majority-control deals, shifting ownership from non-EU to EU investors.
literature.summary_plain: After Germany tightened checks on foreign takeovers in sensitive sectors in 2020, more of these firms were bought by investors from other EU countries rather than from outside the EU.
literature.quality: Clean DiD on national reform that coincided with and partly implemented the EU framework (AWG/AWV 2020 amendments); single-country, effect sizes not in abstract
literature.citation: Kaya, O.; Mostowfi, M.; Sugandhita, S. (2026), Foreign investment screening and cross-border M&A in sensitive sectors: Evidence from Germany, Finance Research Letters, vol. 92, 109525

literature.authors: Agatha Kratz, Max J. Zenglein, Andreas Mischer, Gregor Sebastian, Armand Meyer (Rhodium Group and MERICS)
literature.title: Chinese Investment Rebounds Despite Growing Frictions: Chinese FDI in Europe: 2024 Update
literature.method: descriptive deal-level tracking of Chinese M&A and greenfield FDI in the EU and UK (Rhodium China Cross Border Monitor), combined with Commission screening statistics and a hand-collected list of publicly disclosed screening cases (section 3)
literature.outcomes: Chinese FDI volumes and composition; share of screening notifications involving Chinese investors; outcomes of disclosed screening cases
literature.headline: The share of EU-screened transactions involving Chinese investors rose to 6% in 2023 (from 5.4% in 2022) even as Chinese M&A fell; the authors count 9 publicly disclosed screening cases involving Chinese firms in 2024 (12 in 2023, 16 in 2022), with blocks or forced divestments in semiconductors, batteries and gas turbines.
literature.summary_plain: Chinese takeovers of European companies have shrunk to a fraction of their 2016 peak, while new Chinese-built factories (mostly for electric cars and batteries) are growing. More of the deals that governments review now involve Chinese buyers, and several sensitive deals were blocked or unwound in 2024.
literature.quality: Descriptive monitoring; screening is one of several drivers (capital controls, geopolitics) and no attempt is made to isolate its effect; case list admittedly partial because most reviews are confidential.
literature.interested_party: Rhodium Group is a commercial research consultancy; MERICS is an independent think tank (foundation-funded)
literature.citation: Agatha Kratz, Max J. Zenglein, Andreas Mischer, Gregor Sebastian, Armand Meyer (Rhodium Group and MERICS) (2025), Chinese Investment Rebounds Despite Growing Frictions: Chinese FDI in Europe: 2024 Update, MERICS Report (May 2025), with Rhodium Group

literature.title: Europe's door to Chinese tech investment is still ajar
literature.venue: Centre for European Reform, CER Insight (4 March 2026)
literature.method: structured qualitative assessment with case evidence (blocked or unwound Chinese semiconductor acquisitions 2021-2025) and descriptive FDI data (Rhodium/MERICS, AidData)
literature.outcomes: blocking of Chinese acquisitions in sensitive tech; shift from M&A to greenfield; geographic shift towards member states with looser screening
literature.headline: Since the 2019 framework, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands and the UK have blocked or unwound Chinese acquisitions of sensitive semiconductor assets, but Chinese FDI has shifted to greenfield projects in permissive member states - Hungary took 44% of Europe-bound Chinese investment in 2023 and 33% in 2024 - which the M&A-focused screening framework barely covers.
literature.summary_plain: CER finds that European governments have largely stopped Chinese takeovers of sensitive tech firms, but the screening system, which was optional and uneven from 2020, does little about Chinese companies building their own factories, which now go mainly to countries with weaker screening such as Hungary.
literature.quality: Policy analysis with case evidence and descriptive data; no causal identification; attributes the geographic shift partly to looser screening without testing it.
literature.citation: James Green, Sander Tordoir (2026), Europe's door to Chinese tech investment is still ajar, Centre for European Reform, CER Insight (4 March 2026)

literature.authors: Samuele Greco, Chiara Pollio, Lauretta Rubini, Alessandra Vecchi
literature.title: Screening degli IDE europei e investimenti green cinesi in UE
literature.method: legal analysis of Regulation 2019/452 and its roll-out plus descriptive trend analysis of Chinese green-sector FDI in Europe 2019-2024
literature.outcomes: Chinese green-sector FDI trends before and after the screening framework
literature.headline: The paper documents trend shifts in Chinese green-sector FDI into Europe between 2019 and 2024 alongside the roll-out of the EU screening framework (no effect size reported in the abstract).
literature.summary_plain: An Italian study that describes how the EU's investment-screening rules were rolled out and how Chinese investment in green technologies in Europe changed from 2019 to 2024.
literature.quality: Descriptive only, in Italian; only the abstract was available (no full text in repository); no causal design.
literature.citation: Samuele Greco, Chiara Pollio, Lauretta Rubini, Alessandra Vecchi (2025), Screening degli IDE europei e investimenti green cinesi in UE, Mondo Cinese (journal article)
